newsitem.title: JAPAN: IMF meet to revive woozy Thai tiger opens in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: IMF meet to revive woozy Thai tiger opens in Tokyo.

text.p: Potential donors began a meeting in Tokyo on Monday to discuss an aid package of up to $15 billion from countries and multilateral financial institutions to help ease Thailand's financial crisis.

A deal, underpinned by financial reforms drawn up by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), would produce the biggest loan package for a single country since the international community, led by the United States, offered almost $40 billion to bail out Mexico in 1995.
Participating in the meeting are 13 countries and three multilateral financial institutions -- the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.

Monetary sources in Washington and Tokyo have said that Japan's Export-Import Bank is likely to be the biggest single donor, followed by the IMF, other financial institutions and other nations in the Asia-Pacific region.
Thailand is looking for $12 billion to $15 billion to plug financial holes it created when it floated its baht currency last month after failing to defend the currency from a speculative attack.
An IMF official said some of the countries were attending as observers, but added that the breakdown of which ones were observers was unclear and would be decided during the meeting.
Observer nations might not contribute money to an overall Thai rescue package, he said.

"The meeting is not just something to approve an IMF programme for Thailand. I am sure there will be an explanation about the programme to the participants and they will discuss how much each country can support Thailand," said the IMF official, based in Tokyo.

Thailand, long one of the booming "tiger economies" of Southeast Asia, has already introduced an austerity package to meet IMF demands, raising its value-added tax, announcing plans to cut its current account deficit and closing more than half of the country's financial institutions.

Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya, who said on Sunday he needed at least $10 billion in standby credit from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other lenders, declined to comment as he went into the conference.
Thanong is set to meet Japanese Finance Minster Hiroshi Mitsuzuka later on Monday.
An IMF spokesman said he had not heard whether IMF representatives or Thai officials would meet with private Japanese banks in Tokyo this week.

In addition to government and multilateral support, private Japanese banks -- which have heavy loan exposure to Thailand -- are expected to provide several billion dollars to top up the package, but those figures might be worked out later.
Thailand has nearly $90 billion in foreign currency debt, and Japanese banks are estimated to be owed about half of that amount.
Participating in the meeting with the IMF and Thailand are the United States, Japan, Australia, Canada, China, Britain, France, Germany, Hong Kong, Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and Singapore.
